title: A Faster Way to Find Hidden Pulsars in NASA Fermi Data
paragraphs: For all the talk of a deluge of astronomical data, the bottleneck in Fermi's gamma-ray archive is not information but arithmetic. Fifteen years of freely available observations contain a trickle of photons from each pulsar, the rapidly rotating stellar remnants whose beams sweep past Earth like lighthouse lamps, and that trickle is drowned out by background emission.

Teasing out a faint periodic signal means trying out combinations of spin frequency, spin-down rate and sky position, a four-dimensional haystack that has defeated brute force. "There's just not enough computing power on Earth to do it," admitted Daniel Pook-Kolb, who led an international team based at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics. By NASA's account, a standard processor would need about 600 years to run the previous best method on the target they picked, and that method still missed it.

The team's ingenuity lay in reframing the hunt as the search for the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, a problem familiar from cryptographic research, although the work itself is not cryptography. In Physical Review Letters they report PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times a second, uncovered with roughly 10 hours of processing, a speedup NASA reckons at a million-fold. Yet the achievement should be read soberly: binary pulsars, whose signals are smeared by a companion's gravity, still elude the technique, and Colin Clark's hunch that "tens or maybe even hundreds" more are waiting remains a projection. One new object is a proof of concept, not yet a harvest.

questions.q: What does the article suggest is the real bottleneck in Fermi's archive?
questions.a: Computing power, not the amount of information.

questions.q: What does the "haystack" metaphor refer to?
questions.a: The four-dimensional space of spin frequency, spin-down rate and sky position that must be searched.

questions.q: Why does the writer call the result a proof of concept?
questions.a: Only one new pulsar has been reported, and the larger harvest is still a projection.
